title: Implement stream termination protocol with deadline resurrection and cooperative cancel handshake
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Summary:
We need a robust stream termination protocol in the Go SDK that makes cooperative cancellation between client goroutines, prefetch workers, and the network stream deterministic and ergonomic. The goal is to avoid leaked goroutines, reduce spurious deadline cancellations, and provide a small set of primitives that make it easy for application code to drain and close streams safely while preserving low-latency reads for healthy sessions.

Background / motivation:
- Current streaming examples show races: parent context canceled while prefetch goroutines are still writing to buffers, causing panics or stalled finalization.
- Customers building long-lived streaming sessions (chat, agent loops) need a graceful way to request a fast shutdown that still lets in-flight tokens complete or be checkpointed.
- Runtime improvements (prefix caching, batching) require the SDK to coordinate token prefetch cancellation without dropping useful cached KV state.

Design proposal (high-level):
1) Stream termination protocol: introduce a Stream.Handle with methods GracefulClose(ctx) and Abort(reason). GracefulClose triggers a cooperative shutdown handshake: SDK sends a "drain" control frame to the server, prefetch workers stop taking new requests, in-flight token production is allowed to complete up to a configurable per-stream grace window. After the grace window the stream transitions to terminal state.

2) Deadline resurrection: when GracefulClose is called with a parent context that is near-expired, the SDK can optionally perform a one-time deadline resurrection: it derives a short-lived child context with a normalized deadline (min(parent_deadline + resurrection_delta, max_resurrection)) and uses that for drain/finalization steps. This avoids mid-drain cancellations for common short drain windows (e.g., 500ms). Resurrection is off by default and guarded by runtime flag + per-stream option.

3) Cooperative cancel handshake primitives: internal cancel tokens that are reference-counted across goroutines. When GracefulClose is invoked we publish a CloseSignal; prefetch workers observe CloseSignal and transition to draining state where they finish current batches and stop enqueuing new requests. A finalizer goroutine waits for worker counters to reach zero or the grace window to expire, then performs cleanup.

4) API ergonomics: keep the public API small. Add Stream.GracefulClose(ctx, options...) and Stream.Abort(err). Provide one helper: WithStreamResurrection(ctx, delta). Document edge-cases. Avoid exposing token counters publicly.

5) Backpressure and memory safety: prefetch queue has a bounded semaphore. When CloseSignal is observed we stop acquiring new semaphores and prefer to cancel pending prefetch tasks. This prevents unbounded memory growth during shutdown storms.

Acceptance criteria / tests:
- Unit tests for: GracefulClose when parent ctx deadline < grace window (with resurrection on/off); multiple concurrent GracefulClose calls; Abort preempts GracefulClose; worker counters decrement reliably under contention.
- Integration test against a local runtime shim that simulates slow token production and verifies no goroutine leaks (use go test -race and pprof goroutine count assertions).
- Performance benchmark: no more than 5% increase in p99 latency for normal streaming reads with resurrection disabled; when resurrection enabled, tail latencies for shutdown sequences should improve.

Rollout plan:
1) Implement behind feature flag in SDK (env REDWOOD_SDK_STREAM_TERMINATION=v1).
2) Dogfood internally with internal canary agent (team: platform-internal) for 2 weeks.
3) Enable default to off for public 2.6 release; enable by default in 2.7 after observational metrics.

Migration notes for customers:
- No breaking API changes. New methods are additive.
- Recommend customers using custom prefetch loops to adopt GracefulClose to avoid leaks.

Open questions / trade-offs considered:
- Resurrection semantics: we limit resurrection to a single short extension to avoid abuse (e.g., never extend indefinitely). Trade-off: may still be insufficient for very long drains but keeps API simple.
- Exposing counters vs opaque handles: chose opaque handles to avoid encouraging app-level dependence on internal counts.
- Backpressure drop vs queueing: prefer dropping new prefetch tasks on Close to prioritize deterministic shutdown over completing extra work.
